title: Ming-Chi Kuo: Intel's opportunity to manufacture for Apple is unprecedented; the future still depends on the yield rate of Intel 18A-P
author: F
text:
F

Fred Chen
Moderator

Renowned analyst Ming-Chi Kuo of TF International Securities, a Chinese investment firm, posted on social media that Apple and Intel have reached a preliminary chip manufacturing agreement. This initial collaboration is seen as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Intel to rebuild its wafer foundry business.

According to Ming-Chi Kuo's analysis, up to 80% of the Intel 18A-P process orders that Apple gave to Intel will be used to produce iPhone chips (expected to be the A21 chip), while the remaining 20% will be used for the base M7 chip. This order ratio basically reflects the sales structure of Apple's terminal devices.

In terms of timeline, Apple is expected to launch the base M7 chip using Intel's 18A-P process in 2027. The A21 chip, expected to debut in 2028, will likely use either Intel's 18A-P or the more advanced Intel 14A process. Ming-Chi Kuo points out that Apple's foundry plans with Intel will evolve along with the lifecycle of the Intel 18A-P process, with small-scale testing expected in 2026, mass production starting in 2027, continued growth in 2028, and a gradual decrease starting in 2029.

To ensure the smooth progress of its plans, Apple has already obtained Intel's PDK to evaluate the performance of its Intel 18A-P process. Furthermore, GF Securities predicts that Apple's ASIC chip (codenamed Baltra), expected to launch in 2027 or 2028, will utilize Intel's EMIB packaging technology.

Apple's renewed partnership with Intel is primarily aimed at mitigating supply chain risks. Ming-Chi Kuo revealed that Apple began negotiations with Intel long before the issue of limited advanced process capacity at TSMC surfaced. Apple recognized that TSMC would continue to allocate more resources to AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, therefore Apple needed to find viable alternative foundry solutions as quickly as possible while it still retained significant bargaining power.

However, this does not mean that Apple will completely switch orders. Ming-Chi Kuo emphasized that the vast majority of Apple's advanced process orders will remain with TSMC. The market expects that Apple may outsource the production of its base A21 chip in 2028 to Intel's Intel 18A-P process, while the high-end A21 Pro chip will continue to be manufactured by TSMC.

Ming-Chi Kuo emphasized that the future development of this collaboration largely depends on the speed at which Intel improves the yield of its new manufacturing process. Kuo pointed out that Intel's current goal is to stabilize the yield of its 18A-P process at between 50% and 60% by 2027. Facing Apple's notoriously stringent standards, this tentative order represents both a challenge and a golden opportunity for Intel to rebuild its foundry empire.
